author: Allison Koehler
title: Everything we learned from Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy's first camp remarks - NewsBreak
text:
By Allison Koehler ,
5 hours ago Minnesota Vikings QBs J.J. McCarthy and Kyler Murray | Michael Owens and Patrick McDermott/Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings finally reached the stage of the offseason where J.J. McCarthy and Kyler Murray can start to make their case for QB1. While their first training camp availability didn’t decide anything, both players offered revealing clues about their preparation and comfort in Kevin O’Connell’s offense.
McCarthy arrived at camp trying to separate his current game from the quarterback who struggled through 2025. His 10 career starts produced 1,632 passing yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions, plus 181 rushing yards and four scores. Those are all career highs because his rookie season ended before it began , and 2025 remains his only NFL season on the field.
Murray brings the experience McCarthy lacks, with 20,460 passing yards, 121 touchdown passes, 3,193 rushing yards and 32 rushing scores across 87 starts. His single-season highs came in 2020, when he threw for 3,971 yards and 26 touchdowns while rushing for 819 yards and 11 more scores.
What we learned from Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy's first comments at Minnesota Vikings training camp 1. J.J. McCarthy believes the game has finally slowed down McCarthy said his biggest lesson from 2025 was avoiding “paralysis by analysis,” a fitting diagnosis after an injury-disrupted season in which his reads, timing and mechanics frequently looked labored.
He believes every play call now clicks quickly enough for him to understand its purpose and react when the original design breaks down.
That progress has come through endless work on his timing, rhythm, and footwork. McCarthy compared throwing a football to a golf swing because every small movement must work together, which is the sort of quarterback answer coaches love, and casual golfers immediately understand.
McCarthy also described a new “clarity of mind” before the first full practice had even started. Pads, pressure and live pocket movement will provide a tougher test, but his comments targeted the exact area that must improve if he’s going to take command of the offense.
2. Kyler Murray isn’t wasting energy on Kevin O’Connell’s timeline Murray answered nearly every question about the competition by steering the conversation back toward the day’s practice. O’Connell has selected a target date for choosing his starter, but Murray knows that decision is outside his control -- he can only show he should be it.
The veteran’s approach fits a quarterback entering his eighth NFL season. Murray has no reason to lobby for the job when every camp practice gives him another chance to earn it.
He needs to execute the play call, protect the football, and remind the coaching staff what his athletic ability can add.
Murray even joked that he’s an “honorable guy” during no-contact practices. He won’t pretend a scramble survived when a defender clearly would’ve made the play, although the occasional disagreement and defensive “hoot and hollering” apparently comes standard with training camp.
3. Both QBs have been preparing for Kevin O’Connell’s offense away from Minnesota McCarthy spent portions of the offseason throwing with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and other teammates in California, Tennessee and Minnesota.
Every rep helps in O’Connell’s timing-heavy system, especially for a quarterback trying to make the operation feel more automatic than mechanical.
Murray devoted the final six weeks before camp to daily playbook and script work. New terminology and footwork can slow down even an experienced quarterback, and Murray believes repetition will eventually let him stop translating the offense in his head and just play.
Jefferson offers whoever wins the job one of the NFL’s best emergency options. Murray called the receiver’s standard “greatness” and said he’s grateful to throw him the ball.
McCarthy called his receivers “monsters,” an appropriate review from the quarterback trying to feed them.
Brian Flores will make that comfort difficult to maintain. Murray has already faced Flores twice in regular-season games and expects the coordinator’s exotic looks to improve the offense, which is veteran-speak for anticipating some rough afternoons .
4. Brian O’Neill is already helping hold the quarterback room together Brian O’Neill’s $96 million contract extension gave both quarterbacks an easy topic on the first day of camp. Murray remembered the veteran tackle as one of the first teammates to contact him after he signed, helping the newcomer settle into an unfamiliar locker room.
McCarthy praised O’Neill’s integrity, humor and long-running role as a captain. Protecting whichever quarterback wins the job will remain O’Neill’s most important assignment, but McCarthy also said he “couldn’t be a better guy to be a partner out on the golf course.”
